newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader, Russians face off for Moscow talks.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader, Russians face off for Moscow talks.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin met his security chief Alexander Lebed for the first time in nearly two months on Thursday after giving him a vote of confidence ahead of new talks with the leader of Chechnya's separatists.

Lebed, due to meet separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev in Moscow later on Thursday, was jeered as a "traitor" in parliament on Wednesday when he tried to defend the peace deal he signed with the rebels on August 31.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov was cheered for saying the accord was a humiliating step toward the break-up of Russia.
In a radio address, Yeltsin pointedly praised the way the former general Lebed had ended the conflict in Chechnya.

"My aide Alexander Ivanovich Lebed carried out my instruction and stopped the military conflict. The most important thing is he succeeded in stopping the bloodshed," he said from the hospital where he is preparing for heart surgery.

But Yeltsin, who despite Lebed's requests had not met the former general since putting him in charge of the Chechen conflict on August 10, also warned that there were still problems needing further negotiations with the rebels.
Yandarbiyev flew in to Moscow on Thursday morning for talks with Lebed and, probably, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"It is too soon to stop worrying," Yeltsin said. "The separatists are approaching negotiations very reluctantly."

He added that Russian prisoners must be returned and warned that the troop withdrawal must not lead to Chechens "plundering" their weapons -- as happened when Moscow's forces left Chechnya in a hurry five years ago on the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Yeltsin said Lebed's priority now must be the restoration of a system of government for Chechnya and rebuilding its economy.
But the president repeated the government line that the status and make-up of new ruling bodies should be determined before settling the issue of financial aid.
"We come in peace," Yandarbiyev, a 44-year-old writer, told reporters on the plane bringing him from the North Caucasus.

He told reporters at Sleptsovsk airport, just outside Chechnya, that he would be seeking pledges from Moscow to withdraw all its troops and pay compensation for war damage. He also planned to discuss the exchange of prisoners.
"I expect to take steps forward in the process of the peaceful settlement of the Chechen conflict," he said.
But his demands could run into turbulence.
Many in the government and opposition feel that, by postponing a decision on Chechen claims for independence for five years, Lebed failed to quash secessionist ambitions.
Chernomyrdin, who has assumed extra responsibilities while Yeltsin is in hospital, has given Lebed's deal a lukewarm response and may now play a greater role on Chechnya.
The premier and Lebed, who has overt presidential ambitions, appear to have been jockeying for position in Yeltsin's absence.

The president said a month ago he was concerned about the haste with which Lebed had agreed to remove troops from Chechnya. Generals in the region briefly suspended the pull-out over disputes about the handover of prisoners of war.
Under previous failed accords, Russia had reserved the right to keep a permanent force in Chechnya while removing troops not "normally" based there.
Army commanders have said they would prefer that arrangement but Yandarbiyev has insisted every last soldier must leave.
